title: pcell: the low yield of dying cells is mostly acquired during their life (birth percentile 0.45, last 0.04), so cell-level inheritance predicts death only weakly
summary: Re-reading the pcell-multilevel genealogies (c06's seeds 0-2 and my seeds 7 and 9, T=100000) with each cell's yield percentile taken at fractions of its life instead of only at its last snapshot. Mature cells that will die start at percentile 0.36-0.55 (mean 0.45) at birth, fall to ~0.23-0.36 at mid-life and to 0.02-0.07 at their last snapshot; cells that will split start at 0.54-0.74 (mean 0.63). The inert marker carried by the same particles stays flat through life (0.39-0.51 at birth). Inside a cell, low-yield particles replicate faster (the yield cost), so a cell's yield erodes during its life and the eroded cells starve: this is multilevel selection, with the cell-level differential mostly built within one lifetime rather than inherited. The inherited part is the 0.45 vs 0.63 birth gap.

finding.operator: within-cell particle replication with a yield cost (cy=0.03) and between-cell starvation
finding.control: identical-event inert marker z on the same particles, read the same way
finding.result: dying cells' yield percentile at birth 0.36, 0.55, 0.49, 0.37, 0.48 (mean 0.45) vs 0.02-0.07 at the last snapshot; splitting cells at birth 0.54, 0.62, 0.74, 0.63 (mean 0.63); marker at birth 0.39-0.51, flat through life. 5 seeds.

limits: Percentiles are among living cells at the same time, so late giants (seed 9, claim seed 2) shift them. Splitting-cell birth values exist for 4 of 5 seeds (seed 2 has no birth snapshot for its splitters in the readout). A test that would settle heritability: a parent-offspring regression of fate (death vs split) on birth yield, or an arm with within-cell mutation off (muy=0 after t=20000) where yield cannot erode.
